idiom_name: hand-rolled sequence envelope with an actor-owned buffer, exposed as an AsyncSequence
implementation_notes: Swift ships no messaging middleware, so the three fields travel in an application-defined envelope on top of whatever transport is used (HTTP, MQTT, raw TCP through swift-nio), and an actor owns the per-sequence buffers, exposing the assembled batch as an AsyncSequence. AsyncStream yields values in the order they are produced, so handing the completed group downstream is easy once the size or end marker has been seen, and NIO's ByteToMessageDecoder is the framing point where header and payload boundaries are recovered from a byte stream. The classic structure is the realization because nothing replaces it.
pitfalls: An actor serialises access to the buffers, but awaiting inside the critical section re-enters; keep the group mutation synchronous inside the actor method.
AsyncStream's buffering policy (unbounded versus newest) silently drops or grows under load; choose it deliberately for partial groups.
A ByteToMessageDecoder must consume exactly the bytes it used (buffer.readBytes) or framing desynchronises on the next decode call.
